newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech PSE pledges to improve market transparency.
newsitem.headline: Czech PSE pledges to improve market transparency.

text.p: The Prague Stock Exchange (PSE) on Monday pledged to improve the transparency of the much maligned Czech capital market, stressing in particular the need for the early creation of an independent watchdog.
"The bourse's chamber...confirmed that the Prague bourse will, in the interests of its greater transparency, institute a range of concrete steps," a statement from the PSE chamber said.

"(The chamber) also regards as very important the creation of an effective body for the capital market supervision which would be conducted by an independent institution with all the necessary powers -- a securities commission," it added.

Despite being the most capitalised bourse to emerge from behind the former Iron Curtain, the Czech capital market has failed to gain the confidence of many investors who have long complained about the market's lack of transparency.
Shareholdings and trading are often shrouded in secrecy with at least 70 percent of deals conducted off-market without information on prices, buyers and sellers immediately, if ever, available.
The PSE pledged in its statement to strengthen company reporting requirements, to concentrate trading on the official markets and to improve the settlement system.

Czech legislators answered the calls of some critics in July when new legislation took effect requiring bidders to make a general offer to all shareholders at the same price once their holdings in a company exceeded certain limits.
However, the OECD among others was adamant in its July report that far more needed to be done to prevent insider trading and bring the Czech capital markets up to its standards.
Recently-appointed PSE chairman Tomas Jezek has said the bourse may have an independent watchdog along the lines of the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) within two years.

But the finance ministry, which currently oversees the capital markets, has been less than receptive to the idea which must be ratified by the government and parliament if it is to have the kind of powers Jezek envisages.
